articles.title: Trump renews designation of Nicaragua as an ‘extraordinary threat’
articles.author: John Perry
articles.content: On November 3, President Trump signed an executive order declaring a “national emergency.” The “emergency” is due to “the unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security and foreign policy of the United States constituted by the situation in Nicaragua.” Supposedly, this emergency began in November 2018, has persisted for eight years and is expected to continue into 2027. The scale of the “threat” Here are some key figures by which to judge the scale of the “threat” posed by Nicaragua. First, some basics. The US population is nearly 50 times Nicaragua’s and its economy is 1,400 times bigger, with Nicaragua’s national income (GDP) only 0.07% that of the US. Second, a military comparison. Nicaragua has one of the smallest defense budgets in the Americas, devoting just 0.6% of its GDP ($116 million) to its military. The US, of course, has the world’s biggest “defense” budget at $954 billion or more than 3% of its GDP (see chart), and Trump wants to make it even bigger. Nicaragua deploys around 12,000 military personnel, under 1% of its northern neighbor’s 1.3 million. Third, its military has little or no offensive capability. Its principal duties include preventing drug trafficking, protecting borders, and conducting maritime patrols. The military also responds to emergencies such as hurricanes and earthquakes and protects the nation’s vital coffee harvest, of which the US is the biggest consumer. So, the notion that Nicaragua – 1,200 miles from the south Texas border – threatens US security is clearly absurd. What, then, is the basis of the so-called “emergency” and what has Washington done to stop it in the eight years since it began? US campaign against Nicaragua In Trump’s first term, he signed the original executive order after the US-inspired coup attempt against Nicaragua’s then recently re-elected Sandinista government in 2018. The anticipated collapse of the government in the face of a violent uprising failed to materialize. Trump’s executive order was an integral part of a political and media campaign to ostracize Nicaragua internationally. Bodies such as the UN’s Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) and the Organization of American States (OAS) were instrumentalized to attack Nicaragua’s human rights record, even though they had sent delegations to the country in 2018 that received evidence of assassinations and torture perpetrated by the coup-mongers. Washington started to put the squeeze on Nicaragua’s economy, cutting off access to loans from bodies such as the World Bank and the IMF, worth $500 million annually. Government officials were sanctioned, often on the basis of little or no evidence . Vital trade arrangements were threatened, including its membership in the regional free trade agreement that improves access to the US market. Media campaigns attempted to target Nicaraguan goods, such as its beef exports . Under Biden, the US Trade Representative launched a spurious investigation into Nicaragua’s allegedly unfair trade practices, such as use of child labor. Biden also launched a damaging “humanitarian parole” scheme designed to lure away skilled Nicaraguans, one reason for an increase in their migration northwards. Trump’s second administration imposed worldwide tariffs that singled out Nicaragua for higher penalties than its neighbors. Washington even attempted to damage Nicaragua’s important tourism sector by raising its travel advisory in 2018 to the same level as those for Guatemala and Honduras, where violent crime is much more prevalent. Nicaragua was refused help during the Covid pandemic. Consequently, its tourist trade recovered more slowly than in countries like Costa Rica. Visits by cruise liners, an important outlet for Nicaragua’s many artisan crafts, have never returned to previous numbers. Renewed executive order Despite these hostile measures, Nicaragua’s economy made a robust recovery after the damaging attempted coup of 2018 and the subsequent COVID-19 pandemic. In 2025, Nicaragua recorded the region’s fastest GDP growth, along with low public-sector debt and high foreign reserves. Its 2027 budget forecasts higher spending but a lower deficit. S&P Global Ratings has recently upgraded Nicaragua’s credit rating. Precisely because Nicaragua successfully fended off Washington’s attacks and rebounded, the hegemon was compelled to renew its proclamation of an “extraordinary threat.” According to Trump’s executive order, Nicaragua poses three main “threats” to US security and foreign policy. First was the “violent response by the Nicaraguan government to the protests beginning on 18 April 2018.” These supposedly peaceful protests led to well over 200 deaths, including those of 22 police officers, and caused at least $1 billion of direct economic damage. Arguably, Nicaragua’s defensive actions were much more measured than Washington’s would have been if confronted with similar violence. Second, Trump’s order hypocritically cites the “dismantling and undermining of democratic institutions and the rule of law” together with “indiscriminate violence and repressive tactics against civilians.” In fact, the measures taken by the Nicaraguan government to defend ordinary people and their constitutional rights have largely responded to US-funded criminal attacks and political interference. Third, Trump calls out alleged “government corruption” contributing to “economic destabilization.” Again, this grossly hypocritical charge hardly squares with Nicaragua’s economic achievements or its massive success in improving life for ordinary Nicaraguans. They have seen poverty reduced to under 14%, along with major improvements in public health services, free education, subsidized housing and infrastructure such as water supply, electricity, highways and public transport. The real threat The real strategic threat to the United States is Nicaragua’s ability to improve the lives of its citizens while maintaining a strong economy, despite Washington’s best efforts to prevent it. Trump’s renewal of the executive order signals that these threats will continue. His newly appointed chief of staff, Stephen Miller, identified Nicaragua as an exception to the realignment of countries behind Trump’s agenda for the hemisphere. He euphemistically suggested that the US could secure “a better future for the people of Nicaragua” via its regional alliance, the “Shield of the Americas.” All three of Nicaragua’s immediate neighbors are part of Trump’s “Shield.” Secretary of State Rubio has used the OAS to push Nicaragua into compliance. Although the country is no longer an OAS member, ten Latin American nations have been persuaded to participate. This arrangement could further threaten Nicaragua’s trade links, its diplomatic status and even regional air connections. The OAS is convening again on December 1 to decide how to ramp up this pressure. The ultimate hypocrisy in Trump’s executive order is, of course, that it is the US that poses an ever-present strategic threat to Nicaragua, not the other way around. Nicaragua-based writer John Perry is published in the London Review of Books, The Grayzone, CovertAction and elsewhere. Roger D. Harris is active with the Task Force on the Americas and the US Peace Council . Both are members of the Nicaragua Solidarity Coalition .

articles.title: Hegseth’s impeachment dodge, the draft, & the troops who won’t fight | w/ Mike Prysner
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth dodged impeachment this week thanks to 11 no-show Democrats on Hakeem Jeffries’ watch. Mike Prysner, Iraq War veteran and executive director of the Center on Conscience and War, joins Zoe Alexandra and Rania Khalek to unpack the charges in Rep. Thomas Massie’s articles of impeachment – from an illegal war on Iran that opened with the bombing of the Minab girls’ school, to a boat strike killing spree in the Caribbean and Pacific that has left more than 230 people dead. Opposition to war got Democrats elected, Prysner says, and at the first chance to deliver, “they just completely slept on it.” Prysner says conscientious objector filings are at a 25-year high, and they nearly all cite Minab. Not afraid for their own lives, he says; they refuse to hurt people they have no reason to hurt. He explains why a generation that grew up watching Gaza on their phones won’t fight in Trump’s wars, and why Hegseth’s Christian nationalist, anti-DEI overhaul of the military targeting women and Black soldiers is driving even more troops out. So starting next month, eligible young men will be automatically registered for the military draft. Prysner explains what automatic Selective Service registration really means – and how to prepare. Watch full episodes of BT Live, join breakthroughnews.org as a member today! #breakthroughnews ****** Rough transcript follows: [Speaker 1:] What is set to change on December 18th is that you will no longer have the choice to not register. You will be registered for the draft automatically by Grock or Palantir or whatever AI company. They’re going to scrape the data of Americans and put them on this draft list. It has a lot of problems. It puts you on a draft list when you don’t want to be, making you eligible to be drafted. Even being on the list should be a problem because the draft system was created as a show of force for the US to intimidate and threaten countries around the world. It was created during the Soviet intervention in Afghanistan, where the US was supporting Osama bin Laden. It was specifically a show of force in the Cold War. This week, the US House of Representatives failed to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, thanks to 11 Democrats who skipped the vote. This impeachment motion was brought forward by Republican Representative Thomas Massie from Kentucky. He raised charges around Hegseth’s conduct regarding the war on Iran and the deadly strikes on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific. This failure to impeach Hegseth has opened up a broader conversation about Democrats’ ability to carry forward these promises and what Hegseth has done as Secretary of War, what it has meant for the US military, and his attempts to deify the US military. To talk about these aspects and what it means, we are joined by Mike Prysner, a US Army veteran and the executive director of the Center on Conscience and War. Mike, thank you for joining us here at BT Live. [Speaker 2:] Thanks for having me. Again, on Tuesday, thank you to those 11 Democrats who, for some reason, just couldn’t be present for that vote. Great job, Hakeem Jeffries, just doing his job. It was the outgoing Republican Representative, Thomas Massie, who raised this impeachment of Pete Hegseth for his conduct in the Iran war and these boat strikes. Beyond this failure of the Democrats to carry this out, talk to us about these crimes. Why are the Pentagon’s actions in Iran and in the Caribbean and Pacific illegal? What are we talking about here? [Speaker 1:] It’s a violation of the War Powers Act, which has been going on for more than 60 days without congressional approval. Every administration in my lifetime has done this, especially in the war on terror era. It’s not abnormal, but the fact they are targeting Hegseth over this is significant. One of the main issues is the Minab school bombing, which has had resonance throughout the country and within the military. Of the more than 150 service members since the Iran war began who have filed as conscientious objectors, almost all mentioned the Minab school bombing as significant in their decision. For the administration, they want it to be something they gloss over, but it hasn’t gone away. We still receive calls from people for whom that was a turning point, leading them to take action to get out of the military. That being part of the articles of impeachment for Hegseth is important. His response to that was to hold a press conference saying he was proud of everything that happened and would do it again. The Pentagon’s investigation of the Minab school bombing claimed it was based on old intelligence, saying it was a military target when it wasn’t. It was a mistake on their part. Hegseth isn’t using the typical justification for war crimes. He’s saying he’s proud of it and would do it again, even as the war continues. The US is still launching strikes on Iran and Iranian forces around the world. So, the morning of his impeachment, he said this big war crime, which has caused so much revulsion in the country and the military, is something he would do again. Supposedly, we’re being promised that it’s not the end, and they will try again in January. But people of my generation have learned to have very low expectations. [Speaker 2:] Meanwhile, it’s incredibly frustrating because we’re in this doom loop. One day, there are back-channel negotiations, and Trump says the war is effectively over. Then, as we’re live streaming, Trump declares on Truth Social that the US no longer needs a deal with Iran, halting diplomatic efforts led by Vice President JD Vance. We’ve had you on several times since this war started in your capacity as executive director at the Center on Conscience and War. Your organization has been fielding hundreds of calls from active-duty service members seeking information about becoming conscientious objectors, especially during peak times when it seemed like the war would escalate into a ground invasion. Can you talk about that? I’m sure it ebbs and flows depending on how serious it seems like it’s going to escalate. And not just with Iran. You mentioned the Minab school bombing and the boat strikes, killing fishermen. The US has sent troops to Latin America to expand its military presence. The escalation of war with Iran across the region is intense. What are you hearing now? Are you still getting those kinds of phone calls? Does it go beyond just the Iran war? [Speaker 1:] Absolutely. Relating this back to Hegseth’s impeachment, the Iran war was a consequential factor in the midterm election. It handed the Democrats a historic victory, and the first chance they got to deliver on that issue with the impeachment vote, they completely slept on it. It sets the tone going forward. The fact that it was such a consequential issue in the election, even in deep red Trump states, shows it’s a unifying issue among Americans. People in the military aren’t immune from those sentiments. They come from the same communities that voted big in repudiation of the Iran war. We still get many calls and new clients who have come to this decision. We’re dealing with members of the military revolted by the boat strikes in Operation Southern Spear and Operation Epic Fury, and people directly involved in those operations. We’ve taken clients who were deployed in those operations on the ground in Latin America, part of the Venezuela raid that kidnapped Maduro, part of the boat strikes on the ground in Ecuador, and other places. People who were key in targeting operations have told their commanders they’re not doing this anymore. It’s a big trend that continues. It rivals the trend during the entire war on terror. It speaks to the generation of people in the military today. Most of our clients were born after the invasion of Iraq. They’ve grown up with the war on terror as a background. They’ve seen the disasters where people died for no reason. They were completing their training when the US withdrew from Afghanistan in total defeat, showing that 20 years of fighting was for nothing. They were completing training or entering their military units during the war on Gaza. Young people in the military today saw on their phones the impact of US weapons and policy on a population. That played a massive role in how they view conflicts they’re part of. When the Iran war started with Israel, a country they grew to hate by watching these things unfold on their phones, they realized they had a direct role. If they were morally opposed, they had to take measures to stop. It’s encouraging that we have this level of resistance when there isn’t an active ground war. The last thing I’ll say is it’s a level of resistance when Americans aren’t really getting hurt and dying. There have been deaths and injuries, but the people contacting us are rebelling not because they think something will happen to them, but because they don’t want to be part of hurting others they have no reason to hurt. [Speaker 2:] That’s an important point. I wanted to talk about the culture of the military under Hegseth or the attempt to ignite a cultural shift. We’ve seen these cringe videos posted on the Pentagon and the Secretary of War’s page of him working out at different bases and giving patriotic, nationalistic speeches. Hegseth has spearheaded efforts to root out DEI policies in the military while embracing a Christian nationalist, hyper-masculine culture. Can you talk about the motivation behind this cultural shift and how it has clashed with the growing consciousness among the military ranks? [Speaker 1:] One reason Hegseth is doing this is part of his campaigning for president in 2028, to be this culture war figure. He’s a true believer, coming from an extremist Christian nationalist, white nationalist tradition. His most prominent tattoos are crusader tattoos. He has a chapter in his book called “Make the Crusades Great Again,” advocating a holy war against Muslim countries. That culture has specific views of masculinity, and it’s been behind much of his work as Secretary of War. This isn’t playing well with the military as it exists today. Reporting shows that more than half of people in the military have decided to end their careers early because of Hegseth and the changes he’s making. It’s not playing well with those in the military, but that’s the point. Hegseth is getting rid of trans people in the military and purging black men through policies like the shaving profile. He’s cultivating a religious sector in the military, drawing in people who like his extremist ideology and getting out those who don’t. It’s dangerous because Hegseth wants to transform the military into something that reflects his ideology. What does that military look like? It’s a lot more dangerous and scary than the military today, which is less political than he wants. [Speaker 2:] Congress has made registration for the Selective Service automatic in the 2026 National Defense Authorization Act, signed by President Trump last December. Implementation is due by December 19th, but the agency withdrew its proposed rule in July and hasn’t said how it will meet the deadline. Can you tell us what automatic registration is? Why does it matter, and what does the push to make it automatic tell us about how the US is thinking about the future of war? [Speaker 1:] For over 40 years, since the Selective Service was created, if you are assigned male at birth, you are required by law to register yourself for the draft when you turn 18. But if you don’t, they don’t enforce it. Technically, you can go to prison, but they have never enforced it outside of the early 80s when people publicly refused to sign up. Since then, most young men don’t register, and nothing happens. If you’re not registered, you can’t be drafted. What is set to change on December 18th is that you will no longer have the choice to not register. You will be registered automatically by an AI system. It puts you on a draft list when you don’t want to be, making you eligible to be drafted. Being on the list is a violation of conscience for many, as it’s part of a show of force to intimidate countries. Reagan and Clinton called it a low-cost insurance policy to show the world millions of Americans are ready to be called up. The good thing is they haven’t introduced the regulations for public comment, so they shouldn’t be able to start registering people automatically on December 18th. The requirement for you to register yourself will lapse. But the Trump administration is not known for following the law, and they could start registering people using an AI system, violating the rights and conscience of many. There are things you can do to prepare. The Center on Conscience and War provides information on ways to preemptively plan to avoid being drafted. Being on the draft list itself is offensive to many. The US doesn’t want to use a draft, as learned in Vietnam, but that doesn’t mean they won’t use it. They don’t want to have to use a draft, but they want to be ready. The implementation of automatic draft registration is because self-registration wasn’t working for them. People didn’t want to be registered, so they didn’t sign up. It’s eerie, and in Germany, there’s a massive student movement against a mandatory draft. We’re seeing this trend worldwide, but also a lot of resistance. We’ll come back to you, Mike, in December to see how this plays out. Thank you for joining us on Breakthrough News Live to talk about Hegseth and all of his policies. [Speaker 1:] Thanks for having me.

articles.title: Israel resumes its lethal assaults on Gaza’s healthcare with new massacre at Nasser Medical complex
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: In yet another horrific assault on Palestinian healthcare system in Gaza and a major violation of the US-brokered “ceasefire” deal, Israeli warplanes struck Nasser Medical Complex in the southern city of Khan Younis on Thursday, November 12. The deadly airstrike, which hit the Al-Yassin surgery building at the complex, killed six people and injured dozens of others. Among the dead was a 13-year-old boy and a surgeon, Dr. Rizk Abu Shaaira. Dr. Abu Shaaira who appears in the recently-released documentary “American Doctor”. Nasser Medical Complex: a target for frequent Israeli assaults The massacre is not the first Israeli offensive on the facility, as the site has been targeted in multiple previous airstrikes since day one of Israel’s genocidal aggression on the Gaza Strip. On October 7, 2023, an Israeli airstrike targeted a Palestinian Red Crescent ambulance outside Nasser Medical Complex, leaving several casualties including a paramedic. On March 23, 2025, the surgical department of the hospital was struck, leaving five people killed. Less than two months later, the burns unit within the same surgical department was targeted by an Israeli drone. Palestinian journalist Hassan Islayeh and local police official Ahmed Al-Qudra were assassinated in the strike, while twelve other patients receiving medical treatment were wounded. On May 19, 2025, Israeli fighter jets hit a warehouse at Nasser Medical Complex, destroying 30% of the medical supplies stored there. Three months later, the Israeli air forces carried out a double-tap strike on the complex, killing 22 people. The fatalities included five journalists and four medical personnel. In addition to the repeated strikes, the renowned medical facility, which is deemed the largest hospital in southern Gaza, was raided and besieged between January and February 2024. At the time, Israeli forces had surrounded the compound for weeks, targeting it with heavy shelling and sniper fire that depleted vital supplies of fuel, food, and medicine. The Israeli military also forced thousands of displaced civilians to evacuate the facility, which was their only shelter during the coldest months of the year. Read more: Yet another catastrophic winter in Gaza Between March and April of the same year, Israeli forces renewed the siege on the hospital, which resulted in a complete operational shutdown. After the military withdrew from the facility, investigators discovered mass graves containing hundreds of bodies on the property. Israel uses same pretext, accuses Hamas of using facility as military headquarters Citing the same pretext it already used every time a medical facility in Gaza was struck, the Israeli military announced that it attacked Nasser Hospital on Thursday because Hamas allegedly converted its second floor into a military headquarters. The Israeli forces further claimed that the commander of Hamas’s Khan Younis Brigade, Mohammad Abu Ismail, and a number of the Palestinian group’s fighters were targeted in the airstrike. Hamas describes Israel’s claims as “repeated lies” to cover up a new war crime Hamas issued a statement refuting Israel’s allegations and describing them as “repeated lies” that aim to cover up the crime of targeting a medical facility. “The attacks on patients, doctors, and health workers disproves the occupation’s narrative and exposes its systematic targeting of the health sector in Gaza,” the statement asserted. Analysts viewed this escalation as an attempt by Israeli Caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to prove that he is more capable of “eradicating Hamas” than his rival, Gadi Eisenkot, especially as the latter is racing against time to form a new Israeli government – a race for which civilians in Gaza and other parts of the region would seemingly pay the price. Read more: Anti-Netanyahu bloc led by Eisenkot tasked with forming new Israeli government It is worth noting that Thursday saw the killing of a number of other people in separate Israeli attacks across different parts of the war-ravaged enclave, including Gaza City (particularly near the entrance of Al-Shifa Hospital), Deir al-Balah, Bureij , and Jabalia.

articles.title: Ex-partner of powerful far-right Latin American political operator receives asylum in Mexico
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: Several weeks ago, Latin America listened intently to the story of a Bolivian woman who had been shot on August 17 and, from a hospital, accused her ex-partner of ordering the hit job. Despite the sordid nature of the story, the news made the front pages of several news outlets because the person making the accusation was Nadia Beller, the ex-partner of Fernando Cerimedo. Cerimedo gained political notoriety in the region as one of the most influential political operatives of the far right in Latin America. Cerimedo was involved in several campaigns supporting far-right candidates who went on to become presidents: Jair Bolsonaro in Brazil, Javier Milei in Argentina, and Nasry Asfura in Honduras. In addition, he served as an advisor to President Rodrigo Paz in Bolivia, and his possible involvement in the campaign of the current Chilean President José Antonio Kast is under investigation. Cerimedo managed to become a highly effective operator not only because of his political communication advice and strategies, but also because he was linked to the operation bots farms and was one of the founder of the international right-wing news platform La Derecha Diario. Read more: Attempted murder accusations, troll farms, and presidential connections: the notorious case of Fernando Cerimedo Thus, the charges against Beller were not directed at just another far-right extremist, but at a very powerful individual with connections in the highest echelons of Latin American governments. Cerimedo was arrested by Bolivian police as he was attempting to leave the country by plane, just a few hours after the assassination attempt on August 18. The main reason for the arrest was the discovery of several messages on his cell phone which, according to the prosecution, link him to the perpetrators of the attack against Beller. Following this, Beller expanded on his account of the events and went so far as to accuse Cerimedo of being part of an operation to monitor flights transporting illicit narcotics and of having ties to the highest circles of power in Bolivia. She also stated that these and other accusations were putting her life at risk, which is why she sought asylum at the Mexican Embassy, where she was staying while her request was being processed. On Wednesday, it was reported that the Mexican government approved Beller’s request. For its part, the Bolivian Foreign Ministry reported that it had approved a safe-conduct pass for Beller, who traveled to Mexico on November 11. Apparently, the reason the process was expedited was due to Beller’s allegations that the police were preparing to arrest her for having released audio recordings linking Cerimedo to crimes. Among them are conversations that allegedly confirm Cerimedo’s involvement in appointing public officials, discussing the country’s public policies, and planning police operations. In response, Bolivian Minister of the Interior Marco Antonio Oviedo stated that although Beller has left the country, the investigation into the Cerimedo case (which currently includes four separate probes) will continue. For now, the question remains: will Beller, now safe in Mexico, disclose the rest of the information she claims to have regarding the ties between her ex-partner – a powerful political consultant – and the upper echelons of the Latin American far right?

articles.title: Air quality in Delhi at record low due to Diwali festivities, residents demand measures to protect health
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: India’s capital, Delhi, witnessed a massive deterioration in its air quality over the weekend, making its air unsuitable for human living and a potential public health hazard after the large-scale lighting of firecrackers during Diwali festivities. Delhi was clouded in thick smoke on Sunday and Monday, with various places recording zero visibility with no prospects of improvement in the situation in the coming days. According to India’s Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), during the festivities over the weekend and on Monday, various places in Delhi recorded an Air Quality Index (AQI) of over 400. According to the CPCB, an AQI up to 50 is considered good for humans and anything beyond 300 is considered hazardous and toxic for human living. Delhi and the National Capital Region (NCR) has a population of over 23 million. The AQI indicates the presence of various pollutants in the air at a given time, with each country having its own standards. According to the WHO it is measured as per the presence of Particulate Matter or PM2.5 and PM10 in the air which should not exceed 15 micrograms per cubic meter (or µg/m3) and 45 µg/m3 respectively for a 24 hour period. According to the WHO, the levels of fine inhalable particulate matter measuring 2.5 micrometers or PM2.5 is crucial to judge the quality of air for human breathing. PM2.5 can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstreams causing various kinds of respiratory and health problems. According to the DPCC data the PM2.5 concentration in some parts of Delhi was 993 micrograms per cubic meters on Monday morning, hours after the night of Diwali. The WHO’s safe level says it should not exceed 15 micrograms per cubic meters. Various sources have questioned the CPCB data, claiming it was manipulated to show less pollution in order to avoid public anger and criticism over the government’s failure to control pollution. They claimed the AQI levels to be several times higher than the official levels, with some claiming it crossed the 1000 mark. India’s Supreme Court has repeatedly imposed a ban on the sale and lighting of firecrackers, calling it the main source of air pollution during Diwali. However, the ruling Hindu-supremacist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has been reluctant to impose the ban for populist reasons. Blaming other reasons for the pollution and toxicity of the air in Delhi, the BJP calls firecrackers essential for Diwali festivities. Air pollution is a public health hazard Youth movements and opposition parties have called for accountability over the failures of the government to take effective measures to control the rising pollution levels in Delhi and other major cities in the country. Calling the rising air pollution a public health hazard which affects the poor and working classes the most, Democratic Youth Federation of India (DYFI), a left-wing youth movement, organized a demonstration on Wednesday, November 11, in Delhi against the government’s failure to control air pollution. Various student organizations and members of civil society had held a press conference last week demanding necessary measures before Diwali to control pollution in the city, claiming clean air is a fundamental right of the people. Though lighting firecrackers remains the main source of severe air pollution in Delhi during Diwali , it is not the only source. Delhi has high vehicular and industrial emissions which, during winter in particular, make the air hazardous due to weather conditions. Delhi is one of the most polluted cities in the world. Every year millions are affected and hundreds of thousands of people die in India due to respiratory diseases mainly attributed to rising air pollution. The students and activists also questioned the measures taken by the government to mitigate the effects of pollution on people as “half-hearted” and “knee-jerk reaction” to a perennial problem. Delhi’s BJP government had earlier announced restrictions on constructions and vehicle movement in the city and ordered shutting down schools and asked the workplaces to switch to partial work from home mode during the winter season. Student movements questioned the measures, claiming it completely bypasses the concerns of the poor and working population in the city who face actual challenges to their health and livelihoods due to the pollution. These classes have no means to protect themselves from air pollution and cannot shut themselves up inside their homes due to livelihood issues and their concerns must be prioritized, the speakers in the press conference highlighted. The government should immediately begin a systemic policy change to curb the pollution in Delhi and the rest of the country, including better regulations on industries and vehicle emissions, apart from addressing seasonal issues, such as firecrackers, said K Gopika, vice president of the Jawaharlal Nehru Students Union (JNUSU) talking to the Left View .

articles.title: Scott Colom Wins Stunning Victory, Becomes Mississippi’s First Black Senator Since Reconstruction
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. NERMEEN SHAIKH : We begin today’s show in Mississippi, where Democrat Scott Colom has defeated Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in a stunning upset. Colom is set to become the state’s first Democratic senator in 44 years and Mississippi’s first Black senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction. Colom’s election after three years — comes three years after Cindy Hyde-Smith blocked Colom’s nomination to a federal judgeship. In 2024, President Trump won Mississippi by nearly 23 points. AMY GOODMAN : On Wednesday, Scott Colom gave his victory speech at the historically Black Tougaloo College. He spoke just miles from where civil rights activist Medgar Evers was murdered in 1963 by a member of the Ku Klux Klan. SEN .- ELECT SCOTT COLOM : God bless you. For me, this journey started with a prayer, y’all. And in the Mississippi, our prayers have often changed the course of history. For people that don’t know, the first African American to be a United States senator was from the great state of Mississippi. His name was Hiram Revels. And the way he got to be a United States senator was he was a minister in Natchez, Mississippi. He was elected to be in the state House, and when they were trying to figure out who was going to do the opening prayer, someone suggested Hiram Revels. He gave a prayer that was so powerful that people at that convention decided that he had a voice to be United States senator. That’s an example of the power of prayer. And throughout our history, there are so many people that lifted this state up through the power of prayer in very dark times. But we all know that prayer is only a part of our Mississippi faith tradition. You need faith. And I’ll tell you, throughout this campaign, there were many times where I had to have faith. There were times that I couldn’t get donors to answer the phone; they did not believe a moment like this was possible. But I kept the faith. There were times when I did my first town hall in Jackson, Mississippi. Frank Figgers helped me organize it. Less than 10 people showed up. But I kept the faith. I kept the faith. There were times when I was tired, and I felt like I couldn’t keep going. But I kept the faith. And that is another tradition of our state. There’s so many people that had faith in Mississippi at times where it seemed impossible, people like Medgar Evers. I can’t help but think about Medgar Evers on Veterans Day, a moment like this, where he served his country and came home to Mississippi, when they wouldn’t let him vote. But he had faith that Mississippi could make progress. He had faith that one day everybody would have the right to vote. He had faith that a day like this was possible. God bless you, Medgar. God bless you, Medgar. God bless you. When you talk about faith, you can’t forget Fannie Lou Hamer, who had faith that her being sick and tired could move a nation to understand that places like Mississippi have to matter, who had faith that even after she became a national celebrity and she could have gone anywhere in the world, she came right back to Mississippi. She had faith, y’all. And right now we have several veterans of the civil rights movement who are a part of her tradition of faith. Let’s please give them a round of applause, y’all. AMY GOODMAN : That was Scott Colom, Mississippi’s newly elected Democratic senator.

articles.title: Relatives of Slain Freedom Summer Activists Celebrate Scott Colom’s Historic Senate Win in Mississippi
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : We go now to Meridian, Mississippi, where we’re joined by Angela Lewis, the daughter of civil rights activist James Chaney. She was born just 10 days before he was killed by the Ku Klux Klan along with Mickey Schwerner and Andrew Goodman. The date, June 21st, 1964. They were killed by local white supremacists in Mississippi and buried in an earthen dam, not found until 44 days later. The three had traveled to Mississippi as part of the Freedom Summer campaign to register Black voters. Angela Lewis, thanks so much for being with us. I’m wondering your thoughts today. And as you watched Scott Colom last night accept the vote as the next Democratic senator from Mississippi, the first time a Black senator will represent Mississippi since Reconstruction, your thoughts? ANGELA LEWIS : Good morning, and thank you for having me today. First, I would like to say congratulations to Mr. Scott Colom, his family, and to all of those newly elected officials. I’m very happy, and I just think that this is a day of celebration, not only for Mississippi and for those that won, but I believe that the ancestors are proud and that the work that has been done to get us to this point, it has paid off, and it’s paying off today. NERMEEN SHAIKH : So, Angela Lewis, if you could talk about some of that work? Leon Russell, the chairman of the NAACP board, said, “This is purely the work of particularly the Black community. There was not a whole lot of money, but there was a whole lot of organizing.” Angela? ANGELA LEWIS : Yes, the foot soldiers, the boots on the ground, and those that were making the phone calls and doing the work, those are the people, the unsung heroes, that deserve a lot of credit for the wins. NERMEEN SHAIKH : And Mississippi, as we mentioned earlier, has voted for a Republican presidential candidate in every election since the 1980s, and just in 2024, two years ago, Trump won the state by 23 points. So, what do you think accounts for this shift? ANGELA LEWIS : I think it’s the dedication of the people that stay hopeful and believe that change is possible. And I believe that that’s what we have seen in these recent elections and a lot of the flips and turnovers that we’re seeing. It’s just dedicated people, teachers and the people in the community that’s getting out and registering and getting information out. AMY GOODMAN : I also wanted to get your response to the county that’s named after the first Ku Klux Klan grand wizard, Nathan Bedford Forrest, Forrest County. Colom won. He also won the county named after Jefferson Davis, the president of the Confederacy. Colom won with 70% of the vote. The significance of this? ANGELA LEWIS : It’s very significant. But I just believe that people were not voting for a particular color, a particular party. I believe that people were voting for help. And they evidently saw something in Mr. Colom that made them feel like that they could hope again and that he was the help that was needed. AMY GOODMAN : And I also wanted to ask you about the vote that you took. You’re a psychiatric nurse. You’re speaking to us from work. You voted in Meridian, Mississippi. What did you do when you got back in your car? What did you tell your kids? ANGELA LEWIS : Well, actually, on voting day, I had gotten off from work, and I went to cast my vote. And I sat in my car for a minute and prayed, and I thanked my dad and all of those that worked to make it possible for me to even be able to cast my vote. And when I did cast my vote and I came back to my vehicle, I just had to take a moment again to realize the significance of what could happen in this state and to again just be grateful for those that worked that we would have the opportunity and the privilege to even be able to cast a vote. AMY GOODMAN : And I also wanted to get your response — I mean, you were cited by Scott Colom, your father, James Chaney. The famous wanted FBI poster — or, it said not “wanted,” but “missing.” James Chaney, your dad, Andrew Goodman and Mickey Schwerner, Michael Schwerner, killed in 1964 when they’d gone to Mississippi as part of the Freedom Summer campaign to register Black voters. They were first arrested, held in a jail, looked like there was law enforcement involvement when they were followed and then killed and buried in an earthen dam. You had just been born. Your thoughts about your father fighting for African Americans to be able to vote, what he would be feeling this day, James Chaney? ANGELA LEWIS : I think that he would be, just like the rest of us here in Mississippi, very proud. And I just believe that the day after the Tuesday, after we voted, I believe that next Wednesday, if not the same day, my dad would have gotten up and continued to work and to educate and to register people to vote. AMY GOODMAN : Well, I want to bring in a person you know well, Angela Lewis, David Goodman. He is the brother of Andrew Goodman, who also, along with your dad and Michael Schwerner, were killed in June. It took 44 days for their bodies to be found, dug up in an earthen dam. The call to the White House — it was Lyndon Johnson, the president at the time — was taken by none other than the late, great journalist Bill Moyers, who was working for Johnson. David Goodman, thanks so much for being with us. I spoke to you last night just as Scott Colom was about to speak. Your thoughts as you’re on this broadcast, as you’re on Democracy Now! with Angela Lewis today? DAVID GOODMAN : Well, Amy, it’s — thank you for having us on the show. Hello, Angela. It’s always good to be with you in the spirit world that we live in. My feelings are that we use words often that — like a “blue wave.” If the Republicans won, it would have been a “red wave.” We’re using the word “tsunami” now. This is not a tsunami. A tsunami is a destruction for all. This is a spiritual change of heart, and it wasn’t easy and a long time coming. And the people of Mississippi have spoken, but the people of the United States are benefiting, whether you’re a Republican or Democrat. And we have to cease and desist this divide-and-conquer business, because it’s not in our collective interest as the United States of America. And — AMY GOODMAN : David — DAVID GOODMAN : — [Senator]-elect Scott has taught us that. AMY GOODMAN : David, you never stopped carrying on your brother’s work, Schwerner, Chaney and Goodman’s work, involved with supporting voter registration on colleges throughout the South. Is that right? DAVID GOODMAN : Yes. NERMEEN SHAIKH : And, David, you referred just now to a spiritual change of heart. How do you think this change of heart came about? DAVID GOODMAN : You know, we’re a big country. We’re the third or fourth most populous country in the world, and one of the biggest. There’s 340 million of us, so making a generalization is tough. But there’s a lot of pain in our country. And I travel. I’ve been in every state. I’ve lived in many states. I’m in contact with people all over our exquisite and beautiful country. We’re complicated folks. We’re not a homogeneous race or identity group. We’re diverse. And we get fit into these little boxes: You’re Christian, you’re Jewish, you’re Muslim, this, that and the other. And it’s easy for power-hungry, authoritarian people to come in and drive wedges in between us. And this has caused massive problems. And we got hoodwinked by a con artist who’s in the White House using those wedges to make us fight with each other. And I think the American people are sick and tired of it. I am. And the vote, look, these were just stunning messages. And the authoritarian force, which is heard all over the world, is doubling down. So, we’re not — we can’t stop. We can’t say, “Oh, we won an election. Let’s take a nap and go on vacation.” It’s going to go on indefinitely if we don’t continuously object to authoritarian small group of people running things. And that’s not what happened. I mean, I can’t make — you can’t make this story up. It’s just stunning. You have a person who’s the attorney general of one of our largest states, Texas, who was impeached by his own party and is running. The governor — AMY GOODMAN : But, of course, he lost. James Talarico beat him, and there was — DAVID GOODMAN : He did. AMY GOODMAN : — to say the least, a blue wave in Texas. David and Angela, we do have to go, but I want to thank you both for being with us. David Goodman, the brother of Andrew Goodman. Angela Lewis, the daughter of James Chaney. Andrew Goodman, James Chaney and Mickey Schwerner were three civil rights activists who went to Mississippi to register Black people to vote. They were killed June 21st, 1964, cited by Scott Colom last night in his victory address at Tougaloo College, the historically Black college. Tomorrow, we’ll look at the legacy of Medgar Evers, also killed by the Klan, also cited by Scott Colom as the legacy on which he now will rebuild his state. Coming up, David Sirota of The Lever . Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN : “Nunca Más (Never Again)” by La Santa Cecilia in our Democracy Now! studio.

articles.title: “Don’t F#*k It Up, Democrats”: David Sirota on Direction of Party & Fight Over Jeffries & Schumer
articles.content: With Democrats set to take control of both chambers of Congress in January, Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders says he will not support Chuck Schumer for another term as the Democratic Senate leader, calling for the party to move in “a new and bold direction.” Michigan Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin has said she will not support Schumer unless he presents a plan to govern differently, and several senators-elect have called for new leadership or declined to endorse Schumer. Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen is considering challenging Schumer. Meanwhile, Hakeem Jeffries is facing questions about his leadership of House Democrats after 11 of the party’s members missed a key vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. After “a big win for the populist wing of the Democratic Party, … it would be a betrayal for that election to result immediately in the Democratic Party simply responding by reelecting the same leadership,” says David Sirota, editor-in-chief of The Lever .

articles.title: From Ranked-Choice Voting to Dumping Electoral College: Rob Richie on Election Reform Movement
articles.content: Alaska is the only Senate race yet to be called. Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is narrowly leading Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan with about 86% of votes counted. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, a system where voters choose not only their top candidate, but can also indicate an order of preference for remaining candidates on the ballot. If no candidate wins a majority as the top choice, then second-choice votes are added to the totals and so on until there is a winner. Rob Richie, president and founder of Expand Democracy and a senior adviser with FairVote, explains how ranked-choice voting has shaped the Alaska race and how it is “a system that promotes [candidates] reaching out, engaging, and, for voters, a lot of freedom.” Richie adds that Peltola is “heavily favored to win at this point.”

articles.title: Farmers in India call for another national mobilization
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: Farmers unions in India, under the banner of the Samyukta Kisan Morcha (SKM), have called for a nationwide mobilization to protest the attempt to open the country’s agricultural market for foreign competition without addressing the problems they’ve been facing for years. The protests will mark the sixth anniversary of the 2020-21 protests, in which thousands of farmers had camped on the borders of the capital, New Delhi, for months, forcing the government to withdraw farm laws and promise to address other agricultural issues. Read more: Indian farmers celebrate victory march back home as their historic struggle ends after a year The SKM was born as a united front of farmers unions, representing millions, during the struggle against the three farm laws. In a press release issued on Monday, November 9, SKM claimed that the Modi government has not fulfilled a single promise it made while signing the agreement with the farmers six years ago, which led to the suspension of the movement. “In 2020, farmers numbering in the hundreds of thousands fought the pro-corporate three farm laws. In the signed agreement of December 9, 2021, farmers were given hope that the government will solve” their problems. However, they have been betrayed, SKM said in the press release. Their main demands include enacting a law for the minimum support price (MSP) for all farm products on the basis of the total cost of production + 50% profit formula, scrap all the Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) signed with the European Union, the UK, and New Zealand along with the proposed FTA with the US, and the restoration of the rural employment guarantee law withdrawn recently. The Modi government’s FTAs with Europe and the US will open India’s agricultural markets to highly subsidized agricultural goods which will ultimately harm the livelihoods of millions in India dependent on farming. These farmers are already struggling to continue farming due to rising input prices and the lack of enough return, SKM and other farmers’ unions had said earlier. The November 26 agitation will include the demands of the workers’ unions in the country to scrap four new labor codes introduced earlier this year by the Modi government. The laws are widely seen as an attack on the workers’ basic rights, such as eight hours of work and collective bargaining. Defending democracy The farmers are also supporting the ongoing national agitation against the alleged electoral malpractices in the country. The SKM has also demanded the removal of the country’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of manipulating elections to help the ruling far-right BJP win. SKM’s press release called for the cancellation of the so-called Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and re-inclusion of all the 130 million plus voters removed from the country’s electoral lists through it so far. According to the opposition, most of the voters removed from the electoral lists through the SIR have conventionally voted against the ruling ultra-right-wing and Hindu-supremacist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). They allege that the mass removal of voters was part of the deliberate attempt of the CEC to tilt elections in favor of the BJP. Youth and students groups, along with the opposition parties, have faced massive state crackdown for launching a nationwide movement in October demanding the scrapping of the SIR and sacking Gyanesh Kumar. Farmer’s unions will organize protests at various locations across the country before coming to the capital, Delhi, on November 26 and march to the Parliament while also challenging the Modi government’s attempts to curb popular protests. The November 26 march is set to culminate at the Jantar Mantar in central Delhi, which has been recently denotified by the government as a protest site making it a criminal offense to organize a protest there.

articles.title: France’s protest movement is fighting more than Macron
articles.author: Rania Khalek
articles.content: Macron offered “crumbs.” France answered with a general strike against austerity that brought the country to a standstill and more than 1.6 million people to the streets. Iman D., a student organizer with the Party for Socialism and Liberation, was on the ground at the Paris protests. She tells Zoe Alexandra and Rania Khalek the multinational, multigenerational movement behind the shutdown names capitalism as the problem, not just Emmanuel Macron and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu. Iman explains why Nov. 5 general strikers carried Palestinian flags and wore keffiyehs, and unpacks how Black and Arab youth from the suburbs – the children and grandchildren of the people France colonized – helped spark the uprising. She recounts a visit to a high school in Saint-Denis, where students described unchecked Islamophobia, from the school hijab ban to police abductions from classrooms, and a system that pours money into war while their schools crumble. It’s “continued colonialism,” they say, carried out by forces descended from those that brutalized their grandparents in Algeria. A Minnesota organizer herself, Iman draws the line from Paris to the Minneapolis general strikes against ICE’s Operation Metro Surge. And after the midterms’ blue tsunami that won Democrats control of Congress, she stresses now’s not the time to settle for crumbs: “It’s mass movements that really create change.” #breakthroughnews ****** Rough transcript follows: [Speaker 1:] The people of France truly understand that their fight against racism, anti-Blackness, anti-Muslim fascism, and state violence is tied to Palestine. They’re aware that the same system funding the war in the streets of France against Black and Arab youth is the same system funding genocide and imperialism abroad. They see and understand their struggle as one. Nationwide protests against austerity have continued in France following the massive general strike on November 5th when 1.6 million people took to the streets. Protests are taking place across the country even today, November 10th, and they’re also planned for November 14th, 17th, and 19th. People are not stopping this struggle against austerity and to demand an end to the cuts-based policies put forward by Emmanuel Macron and the government of Prime Minister Élisabeth Borne. Students, trade unionists, and pensioners are all demanding that this government takes seriously the long set of demands they have presented to Macron and Borne. As of now, all of these groups, especially the student movement, have dismissed the offers of dialogue and proposals from this government as crumbs. That’s why they’re staying on the streets. To discuss this massive uprising that has been quite inspirational for people across the world, we are very excited to be joined by Iman D. She is a student organizer with the Party for Socialism and Liberation, and she was on the streets last week in Paris speaking to people about why they’re out there. So Iman, thank you so much for joining us. [Iman D:] Yes, thank you so much, Rania and Zoe. Super excited to join you all today. [Speaker 1:] Iman, you were in Paris last week, witnessing history. Let’s be honest. You saw the general strike which took place on November 5th. Again, there were 1.6 million people according to trade unions that participated in mobilizations on this day. So talk to us first about your impressions of this strike. What was the mood on the streets? And what was it like speaking to people? [Iman D:] Thank you again. On November 5th, France had a general strike, and I had the opportunity to be on the ground and witness it. I don’t even know where to begin. I don’t think I or any American has ever witnessed something at that scale. We were walking for about four hours, and the streets were packed with people on multiple blocks and intersections. There were moments where we couldn’t even move because of the sheer amount of people. There were dozens of different groups and contingents out there, bands playing songs, and chants filling the streets with so much energy. A majority of people there came from different walks of life. The general strike reflected France’s multinational and multigenerational population. It wasn’t just students out there. Talking to the people on the ground—the students, the elders, the mothers, the labor union members—they all expressed concerns around the economic and material conditions in France becoming more detrimental to everyday people as the year has progressed. People mentioned issues with wages, their ability to attend college, access to healthcare, and affording housing and food with rising inflation costs in France. They were telling us that the state of the education system reflects the larger economic issues within the French system. We also saw people on the street tying these economic issues to war and imperialism and the severe state violence and racism against Black, Arab, and Muslim people in France. Even though the media may try to paint it as though people are protesting against Macron and just the government, on the ground, people said these issues aren’t just created by Macron and his government. They were quite literally naming capitalism as the issue and fighting for a new system where people are placed above profit. It was truly inspiring to be on the ground and hear people naming that clearly. Even when we were there on November 5th, there was a perception of, “Oh, what’s going to happen? Is this going to be the end of the movement?” But no, talking to people on the ground, they were energized and determined to continue taking to the streets. As you mentioned, Zoe, they have plans for the weeks ahead to continue blockading their schools. Even this week, many universities and high schools are continuing to be blockaded. Dozens of political groups and unions are pushing for other mass shutdowns in the coming month. It was very clear, talking to people on the ground, that they believe it’s people power that transforms society. The main demonstration in Paris was in an important site in the history of the French Revolution. People in the streets are well aware of that history and know the history of France’s revolutionary past and the history of former colonies of France as well. Many people in the streets come from second and third-generation immigrant families from former French colonies like Algeria and many other African countries. They know that it’s people organizing and taking to the streets that makes change inevitable and will build a new system for them. [Speaker 1:] I’m so happy you mentioned that because it segues perfectly into our next question. We’ve been watching the coverage of the protests in France and covering it here on Break Through News over the last month. Something that’s really animated those protests is the omnipresence of Palestinian flags and keffiyehs. We know these are symbols of Palestine, but they’ve also become symbols synonymous with resistance for movements around the world. We also know that these protests in France have been led by Black and Arab youth from the suburbs of Paris, who are the children and grandchildren of people from parts of the world that France colonized. Talk to us about the connection with the movement against genocide, the struggle of Black and Arab youth in France against racism and Islamophobia, and how that’s all connected in this movement against war and austerity that you’ve been witnessing today. [Iman D:] For myself, being a student organizer for Palestine, I was in awe of the sheer number of keffiyehs, Palestine flags, signs, and banners standing in solidarity for Palestine during the general strike and other demonstrations we attended that week. I got goosebumps seeing people on the streets during the general strike chanting “Free, free Palestine” and connecting all these struggles. When I talked to the students and different people in the anti-imperialist contingents on the ground, many people made the point that Palestine opened up their consciousness. It made them think about the French government and its capacity to commit and aid in genocide, the inflated war budget, while they’re sitting in classrooms with no seats, crumbling walls, no heating, and no plumbing in cold weather conditions. Each time we asked students and youth where the government money is going, they always mentioned war and genocide. For many of these people, a free Palestine means having a better world where they don’t have to experience the racism and abuse they face under the system in France. You brought up the working-class Arab and Black youth. It was them that truly paved the movement we see in France. It started in the suburbs, led by Arab and Black youth. For many of them, they talked about seeing this struggle in France and seeing themselves with the struggle for Palestine. Palestine changed their minds and built this level of consciousness for them, and they were aware that the same system investing millions and trillions in dehumanizing and killing Palestinians is the same system in France investing over 34 billion euros annually in the police system to dehumanize them in their neighborhoods and kill Black and Arab youth every day. The youth described police violence and terrorism against Black and Arab neighborhoods as continued colonialism. They tied this to the fact that cops in France train with the IDF, which is nothing new, coming from America knowing this. These police forces originate from colonial police forces that brutalized their grandparents and killed people in Algeria, North, and West Africa in the 20th century under French occupation. They were well aware that for them, there is no choosing one cause over another or abandoning one cause for another. There’s no sacrificing their language to appeal to a broader audience. These kids were speaking more to international solidarity than their local politicians and anyone else. It was truly inspiring to see and hear that. We also had the opportunity to go to Saint-Denis, a suburb in Paris with a historically Arab, Black, and Muslim working-class majority. We visited the high school there and heard from students about the systemic Islamophobia and racism they witness every day. They talked about the 2004 French law prohibiting wearing any religious symbols to schools and shared stories about having their hoodies pulled down at school if they covered their hair. We even witnessed Muslim girls having to remove their hijab before entering school and the trauma of enduring that every day. Additionally, students shared stories of cops coming into their classrooms and abducting their peers. They showed us videos of that happening and described how cops randomly bag check them in their cities, follow them around, and how one wrong look at a cop can lead to a life or death incident. They said their neighborhoods are literally occupied by militarized police forces. I myself can attest to experiencing police intimidation during my week there. We were stopped multiple times entering and leaving protests, doing bag checks. Our group was circled by cops and forced to do random bag checks, and they even claimed my sister and I had false passports. Witnessing that and hearing those stories and experiences, these youth are well aware that the struggle against state violence they experience in France is the same as the struggle against the war forces that France is investing in. In the US, we see many similarities. Youth across the nation have become conscious and have continued to tie their struggles to the fact that the US war machine is the largest investor in the genocide of Palestinians in the world. College students in the US question why they are drowning in college debt and healthcare debt, not even being guaranteed a job after graduation with the state of the economy, while the country continues to invest trillions in war and the war machine. People have tied their struggle against the war machine to police violence and brutality. The NYPD and LAPD are trained by the IDF. Black people are brutalized and murdered by cops across the nation daily. Our struggles against state violence from France to the United States to Palestine are all one struggle against the same system, which is capitalism. The people of France truly understand that their fight against racism, anti-Blackness, anti-Muslim fascism, and state violence is tied to Palestine. They’re aware that the same system funding the war in the streets of France against Black and Arab youth is the same system funding genocide and imperialism abroad. They see and understand their struggle as one. They’re asking why, in the same way that in the US, we’re asking why our system is investing billions and trillions in police and war abroad and then cutting social services, telling us we can’t afford healthcare for all or housing because we don’t have enough money. The math is not adding up, and people in France and the US know that. [Speaker 1:] Iman, you gave me chills describing those scenes. That is extremely powerful. You are not only Algerian, but you are also Minnesotan. You were on the streets of the Twin Cities for the historic general strikes on January 23rd and January 30th. What was it like having lived through and organized for the Minnesota general strikes and then to see one play out in France? What similarities did you draw, and what lessons do you take from both of these experiences as people across the world face growing inequality, declining living standards, and a seemingly endless desire from the ruling class to wage war and enrich themselves? [Iman D:] As we know, in December 2023, Operation Metro Surge began in Minnesota, where over 2,000 ICE agents were deployed to the Twin Cities to carry out one of the largest DHS operations ever in history. During their time there, we witnessed the arrest and abduction of over 3,000 people. Importantly, we saw the extent of violence that state and federal agents were willing to go to, including the murder of Renee Good and Alex Kueng. After the murder of Renee Good on January 7th, the people of Minnesota refused to back down. They were like, “Enough is enough.” We saw unions, political organizations, student organizations, and even some local officials join the call for a general strike on January 23rd to fight against this. Similarly to the people in France, the masses of Minnesota knew that the occupation of federal agents in their city and these agents killing their neighbors wouldn’t end by complying with Trump. They also knew that public officials like the Minneapolis mayor Jacob Frey or former governor Tim Walz weren’t going to do anything about it, quite transparently, the same way that in France they knew public officials aren’t going to change their conditions. In Minnesota, especially from the memory of 2020 after the murder of George Floyd and millions taking to the streets across the nation to demand change, Minnesotans knew this time again that it takes organization and people taking to the streets to create that change. On January 23rd, we saw this historic general strike where over 100,000 Minnesotans from all walks of life, similarly to France, took to the streets in negative 20° weather. That’s one difference. [laughter] They made it clear who holds power in our system. They knew it’s not Trump, DHS, millionaires, or billionaires. It’s people. It’s working people that hold power. Like France, people are well aware that it’s people that transform society collectively if we take serious organizing and show up in unity. That was such a historic moment. The day after January 23rd, one of the largest general strikes in Minnesota’s history, we witnessed the murder of Alex Kueng in the streets of Minneapolis. It was very clear the message that the federal government was trying to send, which is either comply or be killed. Like the people in France who have been protesting for over six weeks now, the people of Minnesota knew they wouldn’t just back down after this incident. After the murder, I was out on the block where Alex Kueng was murdered because a bunch of people had gathered there. We heard folks chanting “strike, strike, strike” on the ground. I remember people telling me we need to extend the strike to be a week-long strike. I heard people demanding more than that, demanding a whole new system, very similarly to what I was hearing in France where people were saying it’s not just this one issue, it’s the whole system that’s the issue. People were done with state violence and the system that passively allows for this. Seeing all these similarities was very clear with people knowing it’s only themselves that can change their conditions, not one local or political figure. The next day after January 24th, who made the call for the January 30th shutdown? It was Black and Somali students at the University of Minnesota, and the shutdown spread across the nation. In France, the call was made by Black and Arab students in the suburbs. Honestly, being on the ground in France last week, witnessing the general strike brought me to tears. It gave me a lot of revolutionary optimism to see the people power on the ground. Knowing the history of Minnesota and people power there, we can’t let anyone forget about that. They want us to forget about this history. They want us to forget about the history in the US of different movements where it’s people power that made change, like the civil rights movement, like the 2006 Day of Immigration. Seeing all of that together makes me think about how we really have to hold on to our history, remember our history of resistance in the US, and seeing that power in the streets of France brings me optimism. In Minnesota, we saw that it wasn’t like the ICE operation ended and Tom Homan was kicked out because of public officials. It was people taking to the streets and staying on the streets until real change happened. They didn’t do it willingly. They were left with no choice but to end the operation. [Speaker 1:] I want to ask you lastly, given, as I’m sure you saw, people in the US ushered in this crushing blow to Donald Trump in last Tuesday’s midterm elections. We saw this unprecedented blue tsunami, but people were voting overwhelmingly not necessarily for the Democrats, but actually against Trump’s party, his MAGA movement, to register their rejection of many things, including the illegal criminal war of aggression on Iran, their anger about the escalation, the attacks from ICE on immigrant communities, the economic and cost of living crises, many of which are directly resulting from the Iran war, opposition to the genocide in Gaza, which ironically the Democrats also participated in. But all that’s to say, you’ve been on the ground seeing this movement energy. You saw this movement energy in Minnesota. Now that we’ve seen the MAGA movement really collapse since these midterms, as somebody who’s an organizer and who’s in movement building, what do you think comes next in this moment with regard to the US? [Iman D:] When we were on the ground in France, each time we told people we were American, a lot of people asked us immediately about our thoughts on the midterms. [laughter] We reciprocated that question back, asking their thoughts on the US midterms. Many people talked about the midterms in the US and this blue tsunami giving them a sense of optimism against the MAGA movement and this right-wing agenda more than in support directly of the Democratic Party. They connected that with their upcoming presidential election in April 2027, talking about these right-wing forces and Macron needing to be out of office. But they also highlighted the importance of continuing to take to the streets regardless of the results in April 2027. We can acknowledge last Tuesday was a blow to the MAGA movement and the right-wing agenda, showing a clear shift in American public opinion and voting for progressive politicians. It’s clear people are looking for change. But again, talking to the people in France, a lesson we’re familiar with and can bring to the US is that we know it’s mass movements that create change. Now that we see the shift, our task is to hold public officials accountable and push for more, like the people in France. We know that ICE and police violence will continue. The war on Iran is still looming. Rent prices will continue to spike. More and more people will continue to drown in student and healthcare debt. It’s important to remember the power we have as people. Even thinking back to Minnesota, we had Democratic officials in office in the state, and they didn’t do anything to push out ICE. It was people power that did that. As we’re seeing these crises unfold, climate change continuing to detriment our neighborhoods and communities, war escalating with Iran, ICE terror continuing in our communities, and AI backed by billionaires leaving more young adults jobless and unemployed, it’s clear we can’t just depend on the Democratic Party or public officials to change our system. We’re going to need to take to the streets like France to organize and build towards a mass movement demanding a whole change in our system. We know our conditions won’t change unless we do that, and we can learn that through the history of the US, through January, and through the protest movements happening in France. We just have to remind ourselves of that history and continue to organize and build towards a new system. [Speaker 1:] Iman, you have really radiated that revolutionary optimism. I’m feeling pumped. I know we have to go through the laborious task of talking about what’s happened on Capitol Hill since these midterm results, but I think that point is well taken. It will be the mass movement that decides the future and what policies will get implemented, what policies will get passed. Very important lessons to take there. Iman D, student organizer, we thank you so much for joining us here on BT Live and bringing that very vivid recap of your time in Paris because it sounds like you witnessed history. Really powerful stuff there. [Iman D:] Yes, thank you, Zoe and Rania. It was great being able to discuss with you all today.
